headline: The US and China agreed on 26 September to cut tariffs on 30 billion dollars of non-sensitive goods and extend their trade truce to 10 January, the first cross-market news since a Friday close that left the US 10 year Treasury yield at 5.184 percent with CME FedWatch pricing a 69 percent chance of a Fed hike on 28 October.

summary.us: The S&P 500 closed Friday at 7,743.41, up 0.51 percent, the Nasdaq Composite at 27,068.72, up 0.48 percent, and the Dow at 51,828.62, up 0.93 percent, with all three booking weekly gains and the Dow snapping a three week losing streak, led by Microsoft's 3.66 percent rise on a Copilot revamp built around code generation and agentic tools. The 10 year Treasury yield ended at 5.184 percent, its highest since the global financial crisis, after the Fed moved its target range to 3.75 to 4.00 percent in September and 16 of 19 FOMC members signalled at least one more hike this year.
summary.india: The Nifty 50 closed Friday at 23,140.50, up 0.34 percent, and Bank Nifty at 55,580.40, up 0.26 percent, but both finished a seventh straight week lower, reported as the longest losing run since the 2020 pandemic selloff, with the Nifty down 0.88 percent over the five sessions. The driver was IRDAI's 23 September consultation paper on insurance distribution economics, which erased about 14 billion dollars across insurers, banks and distributors, took PB Fintech down roughly 36 percent in one session to its 52 week low, and left FIIs net sellers of 11,490 crore rupees for the week against DII buying of 16,398 crore rupees while the rupee gained 19 paise to 95.80 per dollar.
summary.global: The Nikkei 225 rose 1.30 percent to 66,364.20 for a fifth straight gain after the Bank of Japan lifted its policy rate to 1.25 percent, the highest since April 1995, while the Hang Seng fell 1.01 percent to 24,510.09 in Mid-Autumn Festival trade with mainland, Korean and Taiwanese markets shut and the Hang Seng Tech index at a three month low. Europe was mixed, the DAX up 0.56 percent to 25,408.64 and the FTSE 100 up 0.14 percent to 10,695.30, as WTI fell 2.33 percent to 92.41 dollars and Brent settled at 104.32 dollars on reported US and Iran progress toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

weekly.narrative: The bond market set the terms all week: the US 10 year Treasury yield reached 5.2251 percent on 24 September, its highest since June 2007, and the 30 year touched 5.47 percent, a 22 year high, on strong manufacturing surveys, hawkish Fed commentary and a poorly bid five year auction, which pushed the dollar index to a two month high. Equities absorbed it anyway, because a reported phased US and Iran arrangement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz took WTI down 7.84 percent on the week and because Meta's Muse AI agent kept re-rating the largest index weights, lifting Meta 12.9 percent over five sessions while knocking bank stocks on 23 September as investors weighed whether agents could shop deposit rates on a customer's behalf. India went the other way, undone by a domestic regulator rather than by yields, after the IRDAI consultation paper on insurance distribution economics proposed commission caps and a five year glide path on expenses of management, taking PB Fintech down 33.1 percent on the week and dragging Nifty 50 to a 0.88 percent weekly loss even after Friday's rebound. Precious metals broke their run, with gold off 2.36 percent and silver off 2.77 percent on the week as real yields and the dollar bit, though both recovered on Friday, and copper held a 2.48 percent weekly gain near its 22 September record; crypto diverged from that risk-off tone, with bitcoin adding 3.38 percent and capital rotating into compute and DeFi tokens even after the Bitget hack. Next week the macro calendar is a labour market week rather than an inflation one, with JOLTS on 30 September, ADP and ISM manufacturing on 1 October and jobless claims and factory orders on 2 October, before the RBI Monetary Policy Committee meets 5 to 7 October with the repo rate at 5.25 percent after four pauses.

gcf.outlook_1y: Goldman Sachs Research has a year end 2026 target of 4,900 dollars an ounce, citing sovereign demand and reporting that China appears to be buying more bullion than official data shows. For end 2027, Goldman forecasts 5,400 to 5,600 dollars, JPMorgan and UBS both target 5,400 dollars, and Westpac is at 5,000 dollars.
gcf.outlook_lt: Named house views cluster between 5,000 and 5,600 dollars an ounce for end 2027, with the cited drivers central bank and sovereign buying against the risk of higher real yields. Gold closed 25 September at 4,321.20 on COMEX, down 2.34 percent on the week, and Kitco reported spot failing to reclaim 4,300 dollars into the weekly close as Treasury yields near 5.2 percent and Fed hike pricing capped the rebound. Kitco also reported Wall Street split on the path from here while its Main Street survey stayed majority bullish.

sif.outlook_1y: UBS set a silver path of 70 dollars an ounce by December 2026, 75 dollars by March and June 2027 and 80 dollars by September 2027, in a note dated September 2026, after trimming earlier and higher targets.
sif.outlook_lt: UBS is the named house view at 80 dollars an ounce by September 2027. Supply side context cited this run: industrial demand is projected to fall about 3 percent chiefly on slower photovoltaic offtake, while with mine production flat the structural deficit is expected to widen to 46.3 million ounces and above ground stocks have been drawn down by 762 million ounces since 2021. Silver closed 25 September at 64.245 dollars on COMEX, down 3.47 percent on the week but up 43.73 percent over 12 months.

hgf.outlook_1y: Citi is holding a three month copper target of 15,000 dollars a tonne. Goldman Sachs carries a bull case of 15,000 dollars a tonne, pointing to a structural deficit of roughly 800,000 tonnes a year by 2027. Morgan Stanley has a base case of 11,500 dollars and a bull case of 14,000 dollars a tonne.
hgf.outlook_lt: Named house views for 2027 range from Morgan Stanley's 11,500 dollar base case to the 15,000 dollar bull cases at Citi and Goldman Sachs, with the cited drivers declining ore grades, permitting delays, and demand from electric vehicles, data centres and grid build out. Copper closed 25 September at 6.6955 dollars a pound on COMEX, up 42.46 percent over 12 months and close to the 6.80 dollar record set on 8 September. A fatal accident suspended operations at BHP's Escondida mine in Chile, the world's largest, with no restart timeline.

clf.outlook_1y: Goldman Sachs cut its fourth quarter 2026 Brent forecast to 80 dollars a barrel from 90 and its 2027 average to 75 dollars from 80 after the announced interim deal to lift the US blockade and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. JPMorgan's July outlook had Brent averaging 80 dollars in the fourth quarter and ending 2026 near 78 dollars, moving to the low 60s in the second half of 2027.
clf.outlook_lt: Goldman Sachs published scenarios rather than a single path: Brent above 130 dollars late in 2026 and averaging 105 dollars in 2027 if Hormuz stays disrupted, against an average just under 70 dollars in the fourth quarter of 2026 and below 60 dollars in 2027 on an earlier export recovery. WTI settled 25 September at 92.41 dollars, down 2.33 percent on the day and 7.87 percent on the week.
